text.p: Even Russia's stolid prime minister, Viktor Chernomyrdin, concedes that Russia's privatisation programme -- arguably the world's biggest peacetime transfer of property -- is not all it could be.
"We need reliable rules of the game," he said last week. "Because so far almost every auction causes a scandal."
The biggest scandal of them all broke just one day later, ironically over the one sale billed as open and fair.

The government's announcement last Friday that a Russian and foreign financial consortium had won a tender for one quarter of telecoms holding company Svyazinvest with a bid of $1.875 billion -- far higher than expected -- prompted a furious row in the Russian media controlled by the various bidders.
Allegations of graft and other wrongdoings have flown and First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov -- until now the golden boy of reforms -- was branded "a cockroach".

Controversy is also swirling around the current privatisation of a controlling stake in Norilsk Nickel, one of the world's biggest producers of non-ferrous and precious metals, and the planned sale of most of Rosneft, the last big Russian oil group to go on the block.
Other sales, from oil to insurance, have ended up in the courts, or with the threat of litigation hanging over them.

The winning Svyazinvest consortium includes billionaire financier George Soros and Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (DMG), the London-based investment banking arm of Germany's mighty Deutsche Bank AG, and is built around Uneximbank, Russia's third biggest.
The fact that the result prompted such an outcry does suggest a real contest took place.
Nick Jordan, head of DMG in Moscow, said the bank was proud to have taken part in the Svyazinvest sale, Russia's biggest, and, he argues, most open privatisation so far.
"We believe that we participated in the first transparent auction," he said.
ROW BREWING OVER NORILSK
Another almighty row is already brewing over the sale of a controlling stake in Norilsk Nickel.
The state stake is currently managed by Uneximbank, which is organising the auction and widely expected to win it as well.
Uneximbank says foreigners cannot take part, which would rule out Trans-World Group, the London commodities firm which has already invested heavily in the Russian metals sector.
But government officials say the terms of the sale do not necessarily rule out a foreign bid.

Bids for the tender close on Friday (August 1), but on Tuesday, amid continuing uncertainty about who could take part, Norilsk dropped a bombshell by announcing it was doubling its capital through a rights issue priced at 30,000 roubles a share -- less than half the current market price.

The share price immediately dropped 17 percent, but bounced back on Wednesday on speculation that any dilution from the issue would be restrained by Uneximbank's need to buy up as many shares as possible to retain its stake.
Moscow investment house CentreInvest Securities said in a research note that a fall in the share price before the auction might even be welcomed by Uneximbank.
But whether in the interests of Uneximbank or not, many analysts say the move will strengthen Norilsk's balance sheet, and help it pay off its huge debts.
ROSNEFT SALE SPARKS DEBATE
A bitter debate about the privatisation of oil group Rosneft has led to the departure of several senior executives and a stand-off between the chief executive and chairman.

They now seem agreed on a plan to sell about 97 percent of the company, raising roughly $1 billion and possibly lifting the rule banning foreigners from owning more than 15 percent of oil and other strategic companies.
Potential bidders include Soros, Uneximbank, Russian tycoon-turned-politician Boris Berezovsky, whose group controls the Sibneft oil group, and Russia's biggest oil company LUKoil.
Uneximbank, whose 36-year-old president Vladimir Potanin had a brief stint as first deputy prime minister until March, has done particularly well out of Russian privatisation.

Under the controversial loans-for-shares programme, in which banks gave credits to the government in exchange for the right to manage state shares in partly privatised companies, Uneximbank acquired control of SIDANKO, Russia's fifth or sixth biggest oil company. It now owns most of the company.
SIDANKO has been challenging Rosneft in the courts for years, and mostly unsuccessfully, for the right to own the Purneftegaz PFGS.RTS oil producer.
PRIVATISATION CONTROVERSIAL FROM START

In many cases the winners of the right to manage shares, and subsequently to own them, were close to the banks organising the auctions for the government. And in many cases prices far below the likely true value of the company were paid.
Privatisation became so unpopular that President Boris Yeltsin sacked his economic reform chief Anatoly Chubais, who had masterminded the programme, before last year's election.
The whole process was giving the impression of a carve-up of assets among a small group of well-connected banks and businessmen.

But some of those bankers and businessmen got together early last year to use their funds and the media they control to help re-elect Yeltsin. They brought Chubais, a brilliant administrator and strategist, in to run the election campaign.
Since March, Chubais has been back running economic policy as a fellow first deputy prime minister with Nemtsov.
But the struggle for assets soon shattered the unity of the bankers and businessmen.

Uneximbank's bid for Sibneft, Russia's seventh biggest oil group, was rejected in May, and it has said it will take the matter to court. Berezovsky, who controls Sibneft, was close to the losing consortium bidding for Svyazinvest.

And the bitterness of the row about Svyazinvest in media close to Berezovsky, who says he suspended his business interests when Yeltsin appointed him to the Kremlin Security Council last December, and others in the losing consortium suggests they felt the government changed the rules mid-game.

The Svyazinvest auction was the first to produce a winning bid substantially above the reserve price -- in this case $1.18 billion. This indicates that the government, struggling to pay off billions of dollars of back wages and fund major reforms, had simply gone for the highest bidder, instead of letting the banks take their turn.
The government, dismayed at seeing some of its most influential backers now in opposition, is trying to calm down the disappointed bankers.

"Privatisation does not end with this deal," said Chubais on Wednesday, talking of the Syvazinvest sale. In 1997 "we will have several major privatisation projects including most profitable objects of the oil industry."
